interactions.title: Follow a request hop by hop
interactions.description: Pick a scenario and step through DNS, the load balancer, the API server, the cache and the database; watch the latency add up.

interactions.title: Load-balancing algorithms and health checks
interactions.description: Send requests through round robin, weighted round robin, least connections or IP hash; let S3 crash and see the health-check window.

interactions.title: Cache hits, misses, TTL and LRU
interactions.description: Step through a timeline of requests against a 3-entry cache with a 30 s TTL: hits, misses, expiry and eviction.

interactions.title: Stale data vs active invalidation
interactions.description: A price changes in the database. Compare TTL-only caching with deleting the key on every write.

interactions.title: Cache stampede vs request coalescing
interactions.description: A hot key expires while requests pour in. Count the database queries with and without coalescing.

interactions.title: Eviction policies on your own sequence
interactions.description: Type a sequence of keys, choose a capacity and a policy, and compare hits for LRU, LFU, FIFO and MRU.

interactions.title: Replication, lag and failover
interactions.description: Write, read from a replica, crash the primary and fail over — under asynchronous, semi-synchronous and synchronous replication.

interactions.title: Choose a shard key
interactions.description: Place 24 users with three different shard keys and shard counts; find the hot partition.

interactions.title: The consistent-hashing ring
interactions.description: Place servers and keys on the ring, add a server and remove one; compare the keys moved with hash % N, with and without virtual nodes.

interactions.title: Quorum calculator
interactions.description: Choose N, W and R, write a new value and read it back in the worst case: does W + R > N guarantee you see it?

interactions.title: A network partition: CP or AP?
interactions.description: Nodes in two regions lose contact. Decide feature by feature whether to stay consistent or stay available, and see the consequences.

interactions.title: Build the URL shortener
interactions.description: Make each architectural decision — code generation, storage, caching, hot keys, redirects, failures — and see its trade-off.

interactions.title: Interview simulator: design a URL shortener
interactions.description: Walk the whole interview: requirements, estimates, API, data, IDs, caching, scaling, replication, failures and the 10× question.

interactions.title: Grow the photo app, one failure at a time
interactions.description: Start from one $10 server and fix each failure as traffic grows, ending with the feed design.

interactions.title: Build the video pipeline
interactions.description: Choose the upload path, processing, formats, delivery, protocol and player behaviour for a streaming platform.

interactions.title: Percentiles vs the average
interactions.description: Enter response times and step through the average, P50, P90, P95 and P99 on the sorted values.

interactions.title: A message queue, tick by tick
interactions.description: Watch a burst being buffered, then switch scenarios: consumer crash, poison message, backpressure.

interactions.title: Redelivery after a consumer crash
interactions.description: A consumer dies before acknowledging: see the message reappear after the visibility timeout and get processed twice.

interactions.title: A poison message and the dead-letter queue
interactions.description: One message fails every time: watch it retried, then parked in the DLQ while the rest flow.

interactions.title: Backpressure with a bounded queue
interactions.description: The producer outpaces two consumers; the bounded queue fills and starts rejecting.

interactions.title: Retry storms, backoff and jitter
interactions.description: Twenty clients fail together. Compare immediate retries, exponential backoff and backoff with jitter.

interactions.title: Circuit breaker states
interactions.description: A dependency stays down for eight ticks. Compare blocked threads and calls with and without a circuit breaker.

interactions.title: Rate-limiting algorithms side by side
interactions.description: Send bursts, boundary traffic or steady requests through a token bucket, fixed window, sliding window or leaky bucket.

questions.prompt: Which is a non-functional requirement?
options: Search returns results within 200 ms at P99
questions.explanation: It states how well the system performs, with a number. The others are features.

questions.prompt: A photo app says "uploads may take 3 s, but the feed must load in 200 ms". Where should heavy processing happen?
options: On the write path — at upload time or asynchronously after it
questions.explanation: The relaxed write latency pays for precomputing results, so the strict read path only fetches them.

questions.prompt: Why is "the system should be fast and scalable" a weak requirement?
options: It has no numbers, so it cannot decide any design choice
questions.explanation: Without targets (requests per second, latency percentile, growth) you cannot tell whether a design meets it.

questions.prompt: 43.2 million requests per day, spread evenly. About how many per second?
Responses total 500 MB per second. Roughly what network capacity is needed?
questions.explanation: Multiply bytes by 8: 500 MB/s × 8 = 4,000 Mbps = 4 Gbps.

questions.prompt: 2 million new photos a day at 2 MB each, kept with 3 replicas. Storage added per day?
questions.explanation: 2 M × 2 MB = 4 TB of raw data; with 3 copies, 12 TB.

questions.prompt: After scaling from 2 to 6 servers, users are randomly logged out. The best fix is:
options: Sticky sessions on the load balancer
Sessions in a shared store such as Redis (or signed tokens)
questions.explanation: Moving session state out of the servers makes them interchangeable; sticky sessions keep the state problem and add uneven load.

questions.prompt: A server reads and writes PostgreSQL and keeps nothing in memory between requests. It is:
options: Stateful, because it uses a database
questions.explanation: Statefulness is about what the server instance itself remembers; the state lives in the database.

questions.prompt: A logged-in user tries to delete another user's photo. Which status?
questions.explanation: The user is authenticated but not allowed. 401 means not authenticated at all.

questions.prompt: `POST /users` creates user 77. Which response fits best?
options: 201 Created with the new id (and a Location header)
questions.explanation: 201 signals that a resource was created; return its identifier.

questions.prompt: A client exceeds its rate limit. Which response?
questions.explanation: 429 tells the client to slow down; Retry-After says when to try again.

questions.prompt: Billions of chat messages; the main query is "latest 50 messages of one conversation". Best fit?
options: A wide-column store partitioned by conversation ID
A single key-value entry per user holding all messages
questions.explanation: The partition key groups a conversation; the clustering key keeps it sorted by time; writes are fast appends.

questions.prompt: Transfers must debit one account and credit another atomically. Best fit?
questions.explanation: Multi-row ACID transactions and constraints are the relational database's strength.

questions.prompt: What should you establish before naming a database?
options: The access patterns, relationships, consistency and scale
questions.explanation: Storage choice follows from how data is read and written and how correct it must be.

questions.prompt: "I always see my own edits, even if others briefly see the old version." This is:
questions.explanation: A session guarantee that only covers the writer's own reads.

questions.prompt: A like count goes 12 → 10 → 13 across refreshes. Which guarantee is missing?
questions.explanation: Reads went to replicas with different lag; pinning a session to one replica fixes it.

questions.prompt: Which feature most needs strong consistency?
options: Booking the last seat on a flight
questions.explanation: A stale read there causes a wrong, costly decision (double booking).

questions.prompt: Which operation is idempotent?
options: `INSERT` a new order with an auto-generated id
questions.explanation: Setting a value has the same effect however many times it runs.

questions.prompt: Who should create a payment's idempotency key?
options: The client, once per logical payment, reused on retries
The client, a new one per retry
questions.explanation: The key must identify the logical operation across all its retries.

questions.prompt: "We may lose at most 5 minutes of data." This is a:
questions.explanation: Recovery point objective — the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time.

questions.prompt: A bad migration corrupts a table. What restores the data?
options: Point-in-time recovery from backups and archived logs
questions.explanation: Replicas copied the corruption; backups hold the data as it was before.

questions.prompt: Which statement about CAP is precise?
options: Pick any two of C, A and P
During a network partition, choose consistency or availability
CA systems are the most common distributed databases
questions.explanation: Partitions cannot be opted out of in a distributed system; the choice is what happens during one.

questions.prompt: Write-around caching means:
options: Writes go to the cache and the database together
Writes skip the cache and go only to the database
Writes go only to the cache
questions.explanation: It is the opposite of write-through on the write path.

questions.prompt: Quorum reads see the latest write when:
options: W and R are both more than N/2 — and only then
questions.explanation: Majorities are one case of W + R > N; W = N with R = 1 also works.

questions.prompt: Which is true about replicas and backups?
options: Replicas copy accidental deletes instantly; backups are still required
questions.explanation: They solve different failures: availability vs recovery from mistakes.
